newsitem.title: GREECE: EURO MPS SAY GREEK ECONOMY IMPROVING.
newsitem.headline: EURO MPS SAY GREEK ECONOMY IMPROVING.

text.p: Representatives of the Economic and Monetary Committee of the European Parliament visited Greece in view of the pending decision on which countries will join the European single currency, they told a news conference on Friday.
"This decision will be taken next March and that is what influenced our decision to visit Greece," said Alan Donelly, the head of the socialist group of the European parliament.
The vice-president of the Committee George Katiforis, said Greece is the only country that has stated it will not join the single European currency on January 1, 1999.
"The Greek government has officialy stated that Greece will not make it by 1999. My personal opinion is that other countries, which have not said so, will not make it as well," he said.

The Committee, after meetings with various ministries, labour unions, industry representatives and the European Committee of the Greek parliament expressed satisfaction on the macroeconomic progress so far.
In terms of budget deficit, national debt and inflation Greece has shown improvement and the restructuring of the economy seems to be going smooth, said Donelly.

"The Greek government is realistic. No one tried to pretend that things will be easy. But if the trend in the Greek economic figures continues to be positive, then convergence will be achieved," he said.
He also stressed the importance of solidarity between all European countries ahead of the implementation of a single currency.
"Maximum solidarity must be maintained. The single currency is not an elite club or a differentiation between northern and southern European countries," he added.
All countries whether entering EMU in 1999, which is the first phase, or at a later stage, will be treated similarly, he said.

"There will be no attempt to raise the hurdle for countries that will be left outside the single currency in the first phase. Conditions for entering will remain the same through the second phase," Donelly said.
A Committee representative from Portugal said that when less developed countries progress, richer countries benefit too.

The Committee's German representative suggested that "outsiders", coutries not joining in the first phase of convergence, should form a group with unified demands and press for them. --Margarita Sotiropoulou, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
